lesson.title: Checking Whether the Leftovers Look Normal
lesson.summary: The normality condition asks whether the residuals, not the raw x or y values, are roughly normally distributed, which is what justifies using a t-distribution for slope inference, especially in small samples.
lesson.body:
It's easy to assume the normality condition is about y itself, but it isn't. It's a condition on the residuals, the leftover vertical distances between each point and the fitted line. y can be badly skewed across the whole dataset and regression can still be perfectly appropriate, as long as, at any given x, the scatter around the line is roughly normally shaped. In practice we can't check 'at any given x' with only one or two points per x-value, so we check it approximately using the full set of residuals together: a histogram, dotplot, or normal probability plot, looking for a roughly symmetric, unimodal shape without strong skew or extreme outliers.

Why it matters: the t-distribution used for both the slope's test and its confidence interval is only the right tool when the sampling distribution of b1 is well approximated by a t-distribution, and that approximation leans on the residuals being close to normal, especially for small samples. As sample size grows, this condition matters less, thanks to the Central Limit Theorem, the same reason a one-sample t-test on a mean becomes more forgiving of non-normal data once n is large.

Back to the six residuals from the hours-studied data: 0, 0.2, −0.6, 0.6, −0.2, 0. Plotted as a dotplot, they sit roughly symmetrically around 0 with no residual standing out as an extreme outlier, a mildly encouraging sign. But it needs to be said plainly: with only six residuals, there is genuinely very little information to judge a distribution's shape from. This is one of the more uncomfortable honest truths about this condition: it's hardest to check well exactly when the sample is small, which is also exactly when it matters most.

What a real violation looks like: a residual histogram with a long tail in one direction, a normal probability plot where the points bend noticeably away from a straight line (especially at the ends), or one or two residuals far larger in magnitude than all the others, flagging a possible outlier that could be distorting the whole fitted line. Mild departures from normality are rarely a big problem when n is reasonably large; a small sample with clear skew or an obvious outlier is a real reason to be cautious about trusting a t-test or t-interval for the slope.
